Many Pilates teachers describe the method through six ideas: concentration, control, centring, breath, precision and flow. These are genuinely useful for understanding what a well-taught class is asking of you, but it is worth knowing where they came from: Joseph Pilates did not publish this list himself. His own writing, particularly Return to Life Through Contrology, discussed related ideas, but the tidy six-item list used in teacher trainings and studios today was distilled and popularized by later generations of teachers to make his approach easier to teach and remember. Because of this, you'll sometimes see slightly different wordings or a fifth, sixth or seventh principle added, depending on the school of training behind a given studio or teacher. In practice, the six ideas are still a fair, honest summary of what you're aiming for in a session: - Concentration: bringing focused attention to each movement rather than moving on autopilot. - Control: moving deliberately through a full range rather than using momentum. - Centring: initiating movement from the deep trunk and pelvic muscles often referred to as the "core" or "powerhouse." - Breath:

Is "Pilates" a trademarked name? No. In 2000, a U.S. federal court ruled that "Pilates" is a generic name for a type of exercise rather than a brand, so any studio or instructor can describe their classes as Pilates (Pilates, Inc. v. Current Concepts, 2000). What sets one studio apart from another is the quality of its teaching, not the name. Should I start with mat classes or reformer sessions? Classical Pilates vs. contemporary Pilates: what's the difference? Both classical and contemporary Pilates trace back to Joseph Pilates' original system, but the two schools of thought differ in how they treat it. Classical (or "traditional") Pilates treats Joseph Pilates' original repertoire, sequencing and equipment as a complete system. passages.text: Where that resistance comes from depends on the format: - On a mat, resistance comes mainly from your own body weight and gravity, plus small props like a resistance ring or light hand weights in some classes. - On equipment such as the reformer, Cadillac or chair, resistance comes from springs, which can be adjusted to make an exercise easier or harder and can also assist a movement rather than resist it. A core idea across both formats is that how you move matters more than how many repetitions you do. A Pilates set is usually short (often 6 to 10 controlled repetitions) with attention on the quality of each one: the alignment of the spine and pelvis, the timing of the breath, and which muscles are doing the work. This is different from a training style built around fatiguing a muscle through a high volume of repetitions. What does a Pilates session actually feel like? A typical session is quieter and more deliberate than many group fitness classes: cueing is detailed, pace is controlled, and instructors often give hands-on or verbal corrections to alignment. Breath is cued alongside movement rather than left to happen automatically, and you'll hear specific instructions about where to place your ribs, pelvis or shoulder blades rather than a general "go." It's normal to feel muscles working in places you don't expect, particularly through the trunk, and it's common to feel fatigued through the core and stabilizing muscles without the class ever feeling like a cardio workout. For a full walk-through of what happens from arrival to the end of a first class, see our full walk-through of what happens during your first class. A note on common myths A few claims about Pilates circulate widely but don't hold up under scrutiny. "Pilates lengthens or elongates your muscles." A Complete Guide to the Method, Its Principles and Who It's For By Katherine, Lead Instructor, Certified Pilates Instructor Pilates is a mind-body exercise method built on controlled, precise movement, breath and core control, performed either on a mat using body weight or on spring-loaded equipment such as the reformer. It was developed by Joseph Pilates in the early twentieth century, who called it "Contrology" to emphasize conscious control of movement. The method prioritizes quality of movement over number of repetitions. Key takeaways - Pilates ("Contrology") was developed by Joseph Pilates, a German-born trainer who refined his system during and after the First World War and later taught it in New York City. - It uses springs (on equipment like the reformer) or your own body weight (on a mat) as resistance, with an emphasis on control and precision rather than doing more repetitions. - The commonly cited "six principles" (concentration, control, centring, breath, precision and flow) were distilled by later teachers to summarize his ideas, not written by Joseph Pilates himself as a numbered list. - "Classical" Pilates aims to teach the original repertoire faithfully; "contemporary" Pilates builds on it with current movement science and modified

passages.text: The Origins of Pilates Today, Pilates is widely acclaimed for its broad application for all people, all ages, all fitness abilities; and the results it delivers. Thousands of studios, health clubs and physical rehabilitation clinics feature the methodology begun by Joseph Pilates in the early 20th century. Pilates is considered critical training for professional athletes in the NFL, NBA, MLB, MLS, NHL and many Olympic athletes. It is the “go to” exercise for actors, singers, and models, and a top-trending topic in global media. How it all began Joseph Hubertus Pilates was born in Monchengladbach Germany in 1883. As a child, Joe had asthma and other ailments. He turned to exercise and athletics and studied various exercise regimens to expand his knowledge base. He became enamored by the classical Greek ideal of a man balanced in body, mind, and spirit, and started developing his own exercise system based on this concept. Growing into adulthood, Joe became an avid skier, diver, gymnast, and accomplished boxer. In 1912 Joe went to England, where he worked as a self-defense instructor for detectives at Scotland Yard. At the outbreak of World War I, Joe was interned as a German “enemy alien”. During his internment,

passages.text: About Pilates Pilates is a form of exercise that focuses on developing strength, mobility, balance and body awareness through controlled, purposeful movement. Rather than simply repeating exercises, Pilates encourages you to pay attention to how you move, helping the body work efficiently and as a coordinated whole. Originally developed by Joseph Pilates in the early 20th century, the method has continued to evolve while retaining its emphasis on mindful movement and the connection between body and mind. Pilates can be adapted for different ages, abilities and levels of experience, from those beginning exercise to experienced practitioners and athletes. Joseph Pilates Joseph Pilates described his equipment as a way of providing carefully controlled resistance, encouraging the deeper muscles of the body to work while allowing the individual to focus on the quality of each movement. Central to his approach was the belief that exercises should be performed slowly, smoothly and with the whole body engaged. Joseph Pilates was born near Düsseldorf, Germany, in 1883. Although relatively little is documented about his childhood, he is widely reported to have suffered from poor health, including asthma, rickets and rheumatic fever. Determined to improve his physical strength and fitness, he devoted himself to exercise

passages.text: Pilates Pilates (/pɪˈlɑːtiːz/;[1][2] German: [piˈlaːtəs]) is a type of mind-body exercise developed in the early 20th century by Joseph Pilates, after whom it was named. Pilates called his method "Contrology".[3] It is practiced worldwide, especially in Western countries such as Australia, Canada, the United States and the United Kingdom. As of 2005, there were 11 million people practicing the discipline regularly and 14,000 instructors in the United States.[4] Pilates developed in the aftermath of the late 19th century physical culture of exercising in order to alleviate ill health. There is however only limited evidence to support the use of Pilates to alleviate problems such as lower back pain.[5] Evidence from studies show that while Pilates improves balance, it has not been shown to be an effective treatment for any medical condition[6][7] other than evidence that regular Pilates sessions can help muscle conditioning in healthy adults, when compared to doing no exercise.[8] Description Pilates can be described as "a mind–body exercise that requires core stability, strength, and flexibility, and attention to muscle control, posture, and breathing".[9] In his book Return to Life through Contrology,[3] Joseph Pilates presents his method as the art of controlled movements, which should look and feel like

Some poses are similar in the two disciplines; for example, open leg balance closely resembles Navasana, boat pose; roll over is similar to Halasana, plough pose; and swan and push-up are essentially identical to Bhujangasana, cobra pose and Chaturanga Dandasana, low plank pose, respectively. Both disciplines develop strength, flexibility, and fitness. Pilates, however, emphasises core strength where yoga emphasizes flexibility.[12] History Pilates was developed by Joseph Pilates, from Mönchengladbach, Germany. His father was a gymnast and his mother a naturopath.[citation needed] During the first half of the twentieth century, he developed a system of exercises which were intended to strengthen the human mind and body. Pilates believed that mental and physical health were interrelated.[13] In his youth he had practiced many of the physical training regimens available in Germany, and it was from these he developed his own method.
